summary: Presents an abstract protocol framework for securely moving credentials, such as private keys, between devices and credential servers. It responds to requirements listed in RFC 3157, driven by growing numbers and types of Internet devices. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3760 is a framework for getting a private key from a server onto whichever device a person happens to be using. A credential server holds the key in an encrypted form, the user proves who they are, and the key is sent inside a second encrypted layer so that it stays protected on the way. The framework defines three operations, uploading, downloading and removing a credential, and the security rules both ends must follow.

questions: how do roaming users get their private keys
what is the sacred credential exchange framework
subtitle: A framework for moving private keys safely between a user's devices

tldr.problem: Digital credentials such as private keys live on one device, and a user with a laptop, a phone and a handheld wants the same credentials on all of them. Copying them by hand is impractical, and on constrained devices the usual import and export tools do not exist.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a client and server exchange built on three operations, GET, PUT and DELETE, over a mutually authenticated session in which the credentials travel inside a second layer of encryption. A credential server keeps the protected credentials in a credential store and hands them out to an authenticated user.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework, not a protocol specification: it fixes the vocabulary, the components, the operations and the security properties, and leaves the choice of authentication method and transport to the protocol designers.

facts.label: Components
facts.value: Client, credential server and credential store

facts.label: Protection layers on a credential
facts.value: 2: a passkey for storage and a session key for transmission

today: RFC 3760 is an Informational memo published in April 2004, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a framework that answers the requirements in RFC 3157; the protocol specifications built on it are separate documents.

sections.title: The Problem: Credentials on Many Devices
sections.content:
Digital credentials, such as private keys and corresponding certificates, are used to support various Internet protocols, for example S/MIME, IPSec and TLS. In a number of environments end users wish to use the same credentials on different end-user devices. In a typical desktop environment the user already has many tools available to allow import and export of these credentials, but this is not very practical. In addition, with some devices, especially wireless and other more constrained devices, the tools required simply do not exist.

The document proposes a general framework for the secure exchange of such credentials and provides a high-level outline to guide the development of one or more securely available credentials, or SACRED, credential exchange protocols. The requirements for SACRED are fully described in RFC 3157, and they assume that two distinctly different network architectures will be created to support credential exchange for roaming users: client/server credential exchange and peer-to-peer credential exchange. This document describes the framework for one or more client/server credential exchange protocols.

In all cases, adequate user authentication methods are used to ensure credentials are not divulged to unauthorised parties. Adequate server authentication methods are used to ensure that each client's authentication information is not compromised, and that roaming users interact with the intended and authorised credential servers.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework answers a practical problem: a person has a private key on one machine and wants to use it on another, and the usual copying tools are clumsy or missing. The framework puts the key on a server and defines a careful way to fetch it.

sections.title: The Vocabulary
sections.content:
The document defines the terms it uses. Client authentication information is the information a client presents to a server to authenticate itself, and it may include a password token, a registration string received out of band and possibly used for initially registering a roaming user, or data signed with a signature key belonging to the client. Credentials are the cryptographic objects and related data used to support secure communications over the Internet, and they may consist of public and private key pairs, symmetric keys, X.509 public key certificates, attribute certificates, or application data. A passkey is a symmetric key derived from a password, a password is a string of characters known only to a client, and a password token is a value derived from a password using a one-way function, for example a one-way hash.

Secured credentials are credentials that have been cryptographically secured, for example encrypted or MACed with a passkey. They may be protected with more than one layer of encryption: the credential is secured with a passkey corresponding to the user's password and also by a key known only to the server, which is the credential's stored form, and during network transfer the passkey-protected credential may be protected with an additional encryption layer using a symmetric key chosen by the credential server, which is the transmitted form.

A strong password protocol authenticates clients to servers securely, where the client needs to memorise only a small secret and carries no other secret information, and the server carries a verifier, the password token, which allows it to authenticate the client. A shared secret is negotiated between client and server and used to protect the data exchanged afterwards.

The document distinguishes an account password from a credential password. The account password, and its password token, authenticates to the credential server and negotiates a key that provides session-level encryption between client and server. The credential password is used to derive a passkey that provides persistent encryption and authentication for a stored credential. Although the same password value may be used for both, different algorithm-specific passkeys are likely to be generated from it, because of different salt values, and differing security policies between the credential server and the credential issuers may mean a user has to remember more than one password.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is careful about words that are easily confused. One password opens the account and protects the conversation, another protects the stored key itself. The key is encrypted twice: once with something derived from the user's password, and once with a session key that exists only during the exchange.

sections.title: Client, Credential Server and Credential Store
sections.content:
Three components take part. The client is the entity that wants to retrieve its credentials from a credential server. The credential server downloads secure credentials to the client and uploads them from it; it is responsible for authenticating the client so that secured credentials are exchanged only with an appropriate end user, and it is itself authenticated to the client so that the client's authentication information is not compromised and the user can trust the credentials retrieved. The credential store is the repository for secured credentials. It may have access control features, but those generally are not sufficient in themselves for securing credentials, and the credential server may be capable of splitting credentials across multiple stores for redundancy or for additional protection.

Three protocols connect them. Protocol 1 is used to authenticate the client and the credential server and to download and upload user credentials between them. Protocol 2 is used by the credential server to store and retrieve user credentials, with LDAP, LDAP over SSL or other mechanisms. Protocol 3 is used by the client to store and retrieve user credentials from the credential store, again with LDAP or other mechanisms. The framework describes the high-level design for protocol 1; protocols 2 and 3 are closely related but out of scope and could be implemented with standard protocols. Administrator and credential server protocols are assumed to be server vendor specific and are not the subject of SACRED standardisation at this time.

Clients are not precluded from exchanging credentials directly with a credential store, or with any other server of its choosing, but mutual authentication with roaming users and a consistent level of protection for credential data while stored on network servers and in transit is provided by the SACRED protocols exchanged with the credential server. Depending on the design of the credential server, user credentials may flow through the credential server to the store or directly between the client and the store. Users may also upload their credentials to several credential servers to obtain enhanced availability, and the automatic replication of user information or credential data among several credential servers is beyond the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three parties. The device asks, the credential server checks who is asking, and the credential store keeps the protected keys. The exchange between device and server is the part the document designs; how the server reaches the store is left to standard directory protocols.

sections.title: GET, PUT and DELETE
sections.content:
The client/server credential exchange protocol is based on three basic and abstract operations: GET, PUT and DELETE. The exchange runs through a sequence of steps: connect, where the client initiates a connection to a credential server for the purpose of secure credential exchange; mutual authentication and key negotiation, where using a strong password protocol or equivalent the client authenticates to the server, the server authenticates to the client, and a session level encryption key is negotiated; client requests, which are one or more high-level credential exchange requests; server responses, in which the server performs the operation or indicates an error; close, where the client indicates it has no more requests and the security context is no longer needed; and disconnect, where the parties disconnect the transport connection. Each high-level operation is a series of request and response pairs, and each request must complete before the client issues the next.

Three kinds of value appear in the protocol. SC-x is the secured credential file, which includes a format identifier field and credential data, where the credential data is an opaque encrypted object such as a PKCS#15 or PKCS#12 file. Name-x is an account-defined selector or locator, a user friendly name, used to indicate a specific secured credential; the names stored under a given user account must be unique, and when no name is supplied for a GET operation all credentials stored for that username are returned. ID-x is a distinct credential version indicator that may be used to request a conditional GET, PUT or DELETE; it should contain the server's last-modified date and time and may contain additional information such as a sequence number or a credential fingerprint.

The upload operation, implemented with PUT, lets a client register new credentials or replace currently stored ones, for example credentials updated by the client using key management software. The client and server establish a mutually authenticated session and negotiate a shared secret, the client issues a PUT message containing the upload credential and related data fields, and the server responds saying whether the credential was stored or an error occurred. If the PUT carries an optional credential-ID, the new credential is only stored if a credential with the same name and credential-ID is currently stored, which is a logical replace operation, and the server must return an error if the client tries to replace a credential that does not exist. The response to a PUT must contain a credential version identifier for the newly stored credential.

The download operation, implemented with GET, is how a roaming client gets its credentials after they have been uploaded. The client should authenticate the server, the user must be authenticated by the server, the client issues a GET request, and the response contains the credential and its format identifier. If the client includes a credential-ID, the request is conditional: the server returns the credential only if the identifier of the credential currently stored does not match the one supplied, and otherwise returns a distinct response saying the conditional download was not performed.

The removal operation, implemented with DELETE, requires the credential server to be authenticated by the client and the user by the server. The user then sends a DELETE request containing the credential name, and may include a credential-ID so that the credential is deleted only if the request identifier matches the one currently stored, which stops a client from deleting a different version by mistake. Together the three operations can perform the basic credential management tasks of adding a new credential on the server, updating or replacing an existing one, and deleting an existing one, and their information can guide more complex operations such as user registration, deregistration, changing an account password, or listing all credentials. Uploading a NULL credential where a credential with the same name exists is logically equivalent to removing the previously stored credential.
sections.plainLanguage: Three verbs do the work: upload a key, fetch a key, and remove a key. Each request carries an optional version marker, so a client can ask for a key only if it has changed, or delete a key only if it is the version the client thinks it is.

sections.title: How the Two Ends Prove Who They Are
sections.content:
Authentication is vitally important, so that credentials are accepted from and delivered to the authorised end user only. If an unsecured credential is delivered to another party it may be more easily compromised, and if a credential is accepted from an unauthorised party the user might be tricked into using one that has been substituted by an attacker, for example an older credential of the same user put back in place. Ideally the list of authentication methods should be open ended, and for all credentials the user authentication method and data is defined when a user is first registered with the credential server and may be updated later by the authorised user.

At a minimum, each SACRED authentication method should ensure that the server authenticates the client, the client authenticates the server, the two securely negotiate or derive a cryptographically strong secret key such as a session key, and the exchange of one or more user credentials is protected using that session key.

Strong password protocols may be used to provide mutual authentication and privacy. They require user-specific values, a password token and related values, to be configured within the server, and only a party who knows the password can calculate the verifier value. At connect time messages are exchanged and complementary algorithms compute a shared common value known only to the legitimate user and the server, and both derive a strong symmetric key that may be used to secure the communications.

TLS authentication may be mutual or unilateral, where only the server is authenticated to the client. With server authentication, TLS provides a secure session in which the client authenticates the server and a pair of session level encryption keys is exchanged, after which all client requests and server responses are integrity and privacy protected. The document warns that the flexibility of certificate-based server authentication creates risks that need to be mitigated, notably the need to ensure the user is connected to the intended credential server and no other, and that a faulty implementation of increasingly complex TLS server certificate chain processing could allow a credential server masquerade or a man-in-the-middle attack. It also warns that simple layering of independently developed security protocols produces a complex multilayer protocol that might be defeated by a combination-specific attack.

With TLS client authentication, the server can request client authentication by verifying the client's digital signature, and the client must be configured with at least one security credential acceptable to the server. Other authentication methods with the necessary capabilities may also be suitable.

For the transport, one or more underlying protocol stacks may carry the credential exchange protocols, and although the use of several suites is not ideal for interoperability it may be required. The suites considered are TCP, which needs a custom credential exchange messaging protocol but gives exactly the functionality needed and no more, and most environments already provide the socket API; BEEP, which provides general-purpose peer-to-peer message exchange over several transport mechanisms and supplies the user authentication, session security and session management needed; and HTTP, which provides general purpose typing and negotiation of data representation and is available in a wide variety of server and client platforms, including portable devices, and can be used with TLS for authenticated session-level security.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists what any authentication method must achieve: both ends prove who they are, and a fresh key is agreed for that session. It then compares the candidates, from a password-based protocol through TLS, and the transports they could run over.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations identify general observations and precautions for a framework supporting credential mobility, and a designer should also consult the security considerations in the SACRED requirements document.

On communications security, the password or password verifier should be protected when communicated from the client to the credential server, and the communicated value should resist a dictionary attack; the entity credentials must be confidentiality protected in both directions, with the same resistance to dictionary attack. Communication integrity between client and credential server is required, so that intended client operations cannot be altered, for example from an update to a deletion of credentials, nor may clients be maliciously given old credentials, for example by an attacker replaying a previous credential download. Proper authentication of the client and the server is required to achieve confidentiality and integrity: the server must authenticate the client so that credentials are not mistakenly revealed to an attacker, and the client must ensure the proper identification of the credential server so as to prevent revealing the password to an attacker. There are no requirements on the SACRED protocol itself to support non-repudiation, although the context in which the credentials are used may have such requirements.

On systems security, secure use of the client often relies in part on secure behaviour by the user. Users should choose passwords with a reasonable amount of entropy and protect the confidentiality of their account password, and the client interface should be designed to thwart shoulder surfing, often by not echoing the exact characters of the password as it is entered. When TLS is used, the client interface should let the user verify that she is connected to the intended credential server, for example by displaying identifying components of the server's X.509 certificate such as its name and fingerprint, and a SACRED client should only be configured with the trust anchors it is to use; re-use of trust anchors from other applications such as Internet browsers is NOT RECOMMENDED.

On the server, password verifiers and user credentials must be afforded a high level of protection, with salting and super-encrypting each to ensure resistance to offline dictionary attacks, and credential server keys protected using sufficient procedural and physical access controls. The login should be resistant to replay attacks, and online attempts to access a particular user account should be controlled or at least monitored, for example by delaying or locking the account after a number of unsuccessful logins, or by logging unsuccessful attempts so that an administrative notice is produced once a threshold is reached. Denial of service issues must also be considered: most are a concern for the underlying transport, but service to a user might be denied if the account is locked after numerous unsuccessful logins, and credential servers should be wary of repeated logins to a particular account or of abnormal volumes of requests to many accounts.
sections.plainLanguage: The security rules cover the conversation and the machines at both ends. The key must be protected in transit and at rest, the user must be able to tell which server they are talking to, and the server should lock or watch accounts that are being guessed at.

viz.caption: THE THREE COMPONENTS AND THE THREE PROTOCOLS

items.title: Client
items.text: The device that wants to retrieve its credentials from a credential server.

items.title: Credential server
items.text: Authenticates the client, is itself authenticated to the client, and moves protected credentials to and from it.

items.title: Credential store
items.text: The repository for secured credentials. It may hold access control, but that alone does not secure them.

items.title: Protocol 1
items.text: Between client and credential server: mutual authentication and the download and upload of credentials. This is the part the document designs.

items.title: Protocol 2
items.text: Between the credential server and the credential store, for example LDAP or LDAP over SSL.

items.title: Protocol 3
items.text: Between the client and the credential store, for example LDAP or LDAP over SSL.

items.label: Credential upload
items.desc: Registers new credentials or replaces stored ones. The server answers with the new version identifier.

items.label: Credential download
items.desc: Fetches a stored credential by name. With a version identifier it becomes a conditional download.

items.label: Credential removal
items.desc: Removes a stored credential by name, optionally only if the version identifier matches.

viz.caption: The credential download sequence given in the RFC

messages.label: connect
messages.note: The client opens a connection for secure credential exchange.

messages.label: mutual authentication
messages.note: Both ends prove who they are and a session key is negotiated.

messages.label: GET Name-1
messages.note: The client asks for the credential called Name-1.

messages.label: SC-1, ID-1
messages.note: The server returns the secured credential and its version identifier.

messages.label: GET Name-2, ID-2
messages.note: The client asks for another credential, this time conditionally.

messages.label: No credential
messages.note: The version identifier matches, so nothing is sent back.

messages.label: close
messages.note: The client ends the session and the security context is dropped.
